question.explanation:
We can sketch the graph of $y = \dfrac{1}{x-3}$ as follows:

  1. Take the graph of $y = \dfrac 1 {x}.$

  2. Translate it to the right by $3$ units. This gives $y = \dfrac{1}{x-3},$ as shown below.

From the graph, we see that

\[ \lim_\limits{x \to 3^+} \dfrac{1}{x-3} = \infty, \]

example.title: Infinite Limits of Reciprocal Functions Where the Leading Term Has an Odd Power

question.explanation:
First, we rewrite our limit using the algebra of limits, as follows: \[ \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{7}{4\left(x-2\right)^{3}} = \dfrac{7}{4} \cdot \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{\left(x-2\right)^{3}} \]

For any non-constant polynomial $P(x),$ we have \[ \lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\left(\dfrac{1}{P(x)}\right) = 0. \]

Therefore, since $\left(x-2\right)^{3}$ is a non-constant polynomial, we have \[ \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{(x-2)^3} = 0. \] Finally, we can evaluate the original limit as follows: \[ \dfrac{7}{4} \cdot \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{\left(x-2\right)^{3}} = \dfrac{7}{4} \cdot 0 = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{0} \]

example.title: Limits at Infinity of Reciprocals of Polynomials

question.explanation:
First, we rewrite our limit using the algebra of limits, as follows: \[ \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{-12}{9\left(x+5\right)^{4}} = \dfrac{-12}{9} \cdot \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{\left(x+5\right)^{4}} = -\dfrac{4}{3} \cdot \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{\left(x+5\right)^{4}} \]

For any non-constant polynomial $P(x),$ we have \[ \lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\left(\dfrac{1}{P(x)}\right) = 0. \]

Therefore, since $\left(x+5\right)^{4}$ is a non-constant polynomial, we have \[ \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{(x+5)^4} = 0. \]

Finally, we can evaluate the original limit as follows: \[ -\dfrac{4}{3} \cdot \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{\left(x+5\right)^{4}} = -\dfrac{4}{3} \cdot 0 = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{0} \]
